<system-reminder>
## Stored Secrets
- Before declaring that API tokens, passwords, or cloud credentials are unavailable, run `cortex secret list` to see stored secret keys.
- Use stored secrets with bash inline injection: `VAR="<storeKey>" cmd ...`. The client resolves <storeKey> at execution time and the secret value is not written into the transcript.
- On Windows (PowerShell), the prefix syntax is identical — `MY_VAR="<storeKey>" cmd` — but reference the variable inside the command as `$env:MY_VAR`, not `$MY_VAR` (e.g. `MY_TOKEN="<my-token>" curl.exe -u "user:$env:MY_TOKEN" https://...`).
- Do NOT embed `<storeKey>` directly in command arguments — it must appear as the `VAR="<storeKey>"` prefix so the client can resolve it before the shell runs.
- Do NOT ask the user to paste secret values in chat. If a required key is missing, tell the user to add it via /secrets.
- Do NOT simulate credentialed external-service work when a relevant stored secret exists.
- For delegated credentialed work, use a full-capability `general-purpose` subagent and explicitly tell it to run `cortex secret list` and use inline injection. Do not assign non-GitHub credential consumers such as Databricks, GCP, curl, psql, or aws to Explore.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
Use `enter_plan_mode` proactively for non-trivial implementation tasks. If unsure, err on the side of planning.

WHEN TO PLAN — enter plan mode when ANY of these apply:
- Multiple files to create or modify
- Task spans multiple layers, modules, or components
- Detailed requirements with business rules, formulas, or tiered logic
- Multiple reasonable approaches with real tradeoffs
- Architectural or behavioral impact on the system
- Exploration needed before implementing
- Design choices where user preferences matter

Once you understand the scope, call `enter_plan_mode` immediately — do not continue exploring or implementing.

Do NOT enter plan mode for:
- Small, obvious fixes (typos, one-line bugs, minor tweaks)
- Single-file changes with clear, fully specified behavior
- Tasks where the user specified the exact code change
- Pure research or "what/where is X?" questions with no code changes
- Executing steps from an already-confirmed plan
- Personal preferences or memory/rule saves
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## ctx Commands
- `cortex ctx show all|tasks|memory` — view context
- `cortex ctx discovery add "<sentence>" --title "<title>" --tags <t1> <t2>` — share findings with teammates during team workflows
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## ctx Preferences — Enforce by default. Act on any startup behaviors immediately.
If the user explicitly overrides a preference, follow them and ask: would you like to update or forget this preference?

- [d926af48] UR project enrichment: Tested 3 architectures - (1) Cortex+Brave wins on quality… (148d ago)

A line whose title is followed by … is shown by title only — run `cortex memory show <id>` to read the full content before relying on one. The trailing parenthesis on every line is the record's age, and `no timestamp` means older than the timestamp field, not recent.
Manage these with the memory commands in the `## Memory` block above.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
IMPORTANT: For Snowflake operations, use the `cortex` CLI via bash instead of individual Snowflake tools. ## Cortex CLI
Use `cortex <command>` for Snowflake operations. All output is JSON. Use `--help` on any command. Do not use `snow sql` when an equivalent `cortex` command exists.

**Key commands:**
- `cortex connections list|set <name>` — manage connections
- `cortex search object "<query>" [--types=...]` — search Snowflake catalog objects (table, view, database, schema, function, semantic-view, agent, cortex-sense, app-service, streamlit, external-table, external-database, external-schema, bi-object, business-ontology, stream, stage, task, pipe, skill, plugin) use --help for all supported types; `--types=skill` / `--types=plugin` search the skill/plugin catalog (same backends as `cortex skill find` / `cortex plugin find`)
- `cortex search table-details "DB.SCHEMA.TABLE"` — look up detailed table metadata (all columns, data types, join patterns, usage stats)
- `cortex search marketplace "<query>" [--marketplace-type=TYPE]` — search Snowflake Marketplace listings (TYPE: public (default), internal, or all)
- `cortex semantic-views discover|list|describe|search|ddl` — semantic view discovery (IMPORTANT***: Search for semantic views BEFORE writing SQL to answer data centric questions)
- `cortex search docs "<query>"` — search Snowflake docs. IMPORTANT: run this FIRST for ANY Snowflake question — your built-in knowledge is often stale, so answer from results, not memory. Output is bounded and multi-line; do NOT pipe it through `head`. If a result's content is truncated, use web_fetch on that result's Markdown URL to read the full page, or grep the offloaded output file when web_fetch is unavailable.
- `cortex reflect <file.yaml> [--target-schema DB.SCHEMA]` — validate semantic models
- `cortex agents discover|list|describe|search` — agent discovery (check BEFORE writing complex queries)
- `cortex lineage <DB.SCHEMA.NAME> [--direction upstream|downstream|both] [--distance 1..5] [--tree]` — list upstream sources/downstream consumers; use before refactoring/deprecating and to find pre-aggregated rollups for analytical SQL
- `cortex analyst query "<question>" --model=<yaml>|--view=<view>` — query via Cortex Analyst
- `cortex artifact create notebook|file <name> <path>` — upload artifacts
- `cortex env detect [--dir=<path>]` — detect Python environment
- `cortex secret store|list|delete` — manage secrets

Do NOT use `cortex fdbt` — use the native `fdbt` tool instead.
Do NOT use `cortex --bypass --print` - use your built-in mechanisms to execute SQL or run a subagent instead.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Snowflake Object Discovery

When the task requires finding or identifying a Snowflake object/asset and the user has NOT pinned an exact identifier, delegate to the `snowflake-object-discovery` subagent to locate it — this is the default and expected way to find objects, ahead of hand-rolling `cortex search` or writing exploratory SQL yourself. It covers any supported object: tables, views, semantic views, Cortex Agents, Streamlit apps, functions, databases/schemas, BI objects, streams, stages, tasks, pipes, and Marketplace listings. 

For ANY analytical SQL — aggregations, counts, DAU/MAU, time-series, dashboards, "find X by Y", "what tables track…" — delegate FIRST to find the right table/semantic view, then write SQL against what it returns.

Run discovery to ground yourself BEFORE answering with ad-hoc INFORMATION_SCHEMA/ACCOUNT_USAGE SQL, and before building anything new.

A display name is NOT a pinned identifier: values like `Northstar` or `Annual Report` still need discovery — only an exact FQN or object name counts as pinned.

```
task(subagent_type: "snowflake-object-discovery", prompt: "Find the best object for: <user request verbatim>\n\nno_discovery_reminder: true")
```

- ALWAYS include the literal `no_discovery_reminder: true`. Pass only what the user explicitly said — add no interpretation of your own.
- The reply leads with a structured Primary block (`primary_identifier`, `object_type`, and an `agentId`) plus optional alternates. Use the `primary_identifier` **exactly as written** — never invent, swap, or re-canonicalize database/schema/name segments, and do not substitute an alternate. The subagent saw all the options and chose this one.
- If you believe the primary is wrong (columns do not support the metric, the object is the wrong type, or your SQL returns nothing), do NOT pick another identifier yourself — resume the SAME session with `resume: "<agentId>"` and a refined prompt explaining what went wrong. Resuming keeps prior inspection state and is cheaper.
- When you present the answer, name the object FQN(s) you relied on — even for analytical or single-number answers — so it is clear which asset produced the result.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
You have `tgrep` for semantic/keyword code search — prefer it over grep/glob for finding relevant files by meaning. tgrep loads on demand: if it isn't already in your available tools, use tool_search to load it FIRST, then call `tgrep` with a `query`. Do not call tgrep before it is loaded.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Cron
Tools: cron_create (5-field cron + prompt), cron_delete (by ID), cron_list. Session-scoped, local timezone, max 50, 3-day expiry. Users can also use /loop.
Pick by lifetime, not wording: cron is for checks that only matter while this session is open (polling a build, re-checking while you work). If the work should keep running after the session ends (a recurring report, monitor, or "ping me every hour" digest), use a cloud automation instead: load the `automation` skill. It runs in a Snowflake sandbox with no expiry, but without this machine's files or local MCP servers. If the lifetime is unclear, ask.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
Current active SQL connection set by user: `gcp` (Snowflake). Use sql_execute for database queries against this connection unless the user specifies otherwise.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
CRITICAL SKILL USAGE RULES:

1. Check if the user's query matches any skill available through the skill tool. If a relevant skill exists, you MUST invoke the skill tool with input { "skill": "<skill-name>" } as your FIRST action BEFORE generating any response or using any other tools.

2. TEAM/TEAMMATE PRIORITY: If the user's message contains team language such as "use teammates", "using teammates", "use a team", "work in parallel with agents", "delegate to teammates", "swarm this", "swarm", "team up on this", "team up", "orchestrate with subagents", "subagent-orchestrated", "gated workflow", "multi-phase workflow", "coordinate agents", "spawn workers", "worker/verifier", "parallel agents", or "run as a team", team-workflow takes priority over domain-specific skills. In CoCo CLI this workflow may already be auto-activated for the turn; if not, load it first. team-workflow controls orchestration, and domain skills are loaded later by subagents.

3. For authoritative information about Cortex Code capabilities, commands, shortcuts, and configuration, invoke the cortex-code-guide skill. It contains an auto-generated reference derived from the current source code.

4. Skills contain specialized, up-to-date knowledge that direct tool use cannot replicate. DO NOT use bash to look for skill files - use the skill tool instead.

SKILL MAINTENANCE RULES:
If you discover a loaded skill has incorrect, outdated, or missing instructions, patch it via skill_manage. Prefer patching an existing skill over any other action.
</system-reminder>

This is a READ-ONLY planning task. You are STRICTLY PROHIBITED from:
- Creating new files (no Write, touch, or file creation of any kind)

Your role is EXCLUSIVELY to explore the codebase and design an implementation plan. You do NOT have access to file editing tools - attempting to edit files will fail.

**ALLOWED** (read-only operations):
- Read, Glob, Grep tools for exploring the codebase
- Task tool with subagent_type="Explore" or "Plan" for parallel codebase exploration (up to 3 concurrent agents — only when investigating genuinely different areas, each with a clearly distinct search target)
- web_search, web_fetch for research
- sql_execute for read-only queries (SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN) or with only_compile=true sql compilation (which compiles only and does not run sql)
- Bash for read-only commands ONLY: ls, git status, git log, git diff, find, cat, head, tail
- ask_user_question for targeted clarifications during research

**NOT ALLOWED** (mutating operations):
- Edit, Write tools (creating or modifying files)
- Bash commands that modify files or state: mkdir, touch, rm, cp, mv, git add, git commit, npm install, pip install, or any redirect operators (>, >>) or heredocs
- sql_execute with DDL/DML and only_compile=false: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, TRUNCATE, COPY INTO
- notebook_actions with mutating actions: insert_cell, edit_cell, delete_cell, execute_cell
- Task tool with subagent_type="general-purpose" (can make changes)
- Git commits, pushes, or other version control changes

While plan mode is active, you MUST NOT make any edits, run any non-readonly tools (including changing configs or making commits), or otherwise make any changes to the system. While in plan mode, this supersedes any earlier instructions you have received (for example, to make edits).

**When to use ask_user_question vs exit_plan_mode:**
- Use ask_user_question for targeted clarifications DURING research — e.g., ambiguous requirements, choosing between approaches that need user preference, or confirming assumptions before designing the plan
- Use exit_plan_mode ONLY when your full plan is ready to present for confirmation
- Do NOT call exit_plan_mode just to ask a question — use ask_user_question instead

**Your process (5 phases):**
1. **Understand** — Read files referenced in the prompt, understand the user's requirements and constraints. Ask clarifying questions via ask_user_question if requirements are ambiguous.
2. **Explore** — Use Glob, Grep, and Read to find existing patterns, conventions, and integration points. Launch up to 3 concurrent Explore subagents when investigating genuinely different areas of the codebase.
3. **Analyze** — Identify dependencies, potential issues, edge cases, and trade-offs between approaches. Trace through relevant code paths end-to-end.
4. **Design** — Create a concrete implementation plan that follows existing patterns and conventions. Consider what could go wrong and how to verify correctness.
5. **Present** — Call exit_plan_mode with the complete plan for user confirmation.

**Required in your plan output:**
Structure your plan with these sections:

1. **Context**: What you explored, key findings, existing patterns identified
2. **Implementation steps**: Concrete, ordered steps for the changes
3. **Verification**: How to verify the changes work — tests to run, commands to execute, manual checks
4. **Critical Files**: 3-5 files most critical for implementation:
   - path/to/file1.ts - [Brief reason, e.g. "Core logic to modify"]
   - path/to/file2.ts - [Brief reason, e.g. "Interfaces to implement"]
   - path/to/file3.ts - [Brief reason, e.g. "Pattern to follow"]

Do NOT make any file changes or run any tools that modify the system state in any way until the user has confirmed the plan.

57... ## 2. What the examples were hiding (learnings from hand-optimizing)
58... 
59... Each row: the original program's cost, what made it slow, and what that means for the optimizer.
60... 
61... | Example | Cycles orig → hand **[M]** | Hidden lesson |
62... |---|---|---|
63... | q0001 | 13766 → 1703 (8.1×) | 52% of the cycles are CAT and LEFT building a label for rows a later filter throws away. **Order of work matters more than the work itself.** `SORT` on `lines` is a no-op because of the `sorted` constraint. `GE l_qty,1` is always TRUE because of `not_null` + `check`. |
64... | q0002 | 3617 → 2011 (1.8×) | The self-join's *counted* side must stay unfiltered. Filtering it too is the naive bug (`q0002.naive`, caught on 17 datasets). Only the outer side may shrink. |
65... | q0003 | 8562 → 2817 (3.0×; 37× on large) | A "count of better rows" self-join is O(n²) per group. A sort plus per-group rank is linear. The HJOIN silently drops NULL and `''`→NULL keys, and the rewrite must reproduce that. |
66... | q0004 | 18442 → 2179 (8.5×; 47× on large) | 36% of the cycles are GATHER fan-out across 4 joins. A SORT before GALL/GSUM is useless. **`customers` has no key**, so de-duplicating `c_id` is wrong (`q0004.naive`). |
67... | q0005 | 5518 → 3294 (1.7×) | Join, then sort, then GROUP de-dup is really a **semi-join**. De-duplicate the small side first. |
68... | q0006 | 6338 → 2091 (3.0×; 20× on large) | A self-join followed by GMAX is GROUP + GMAX + GID. GROUP puts NULLs in one group but HJOIN never matches them, so an explicit NULL filter is required (`q0006.naive`). |
69... | q0007 | 2596 → 637 (4.1×) | Filter first, then TOPK instead of SORT, then build the label for 5 rows. The example data has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts, so `TOPK 4` and a flipped tie-break both **passed on the example data**. |
70... | q0008 | 1524 → 1249 (1.2×) | Already tight. Dead loads are the only waste. Not every legacy program is slow. |
71... 
72... **Cross-cutting.**
73... 1. The biggest wins are generic, and the clever rewrites are the riskiest:
74...    - The generic wins are filter-first, late materialization, GATHER sinking, dead-code elimination, and TOPK instead of SORT.
75...    - The self-join idioms give the largest gains on large data, and they are also the riskiest.
76... 2. Constraints carry the correctness argument:
77...    - `not_null` + `refs` to a `key` means exactly one match.
78...    - `sorted` means a SORT on those keys is a no-op.
79...    - A table with **no key** can fan out a join.
80... 3. **Weak data hides bugs.**
81...    - A q0004 baseline was missed until the generator planted the programs' own literals (`'KITCHEN'`).
82...    - Every gain is relative to the data: on small datasets speedups shrink to 1.2–3× because the filter results are often empty.
83...

86... ## 3. Optimizer design
87... 
88... **Pipeline.**
89... 1. Parse into an SSA IR.
90... 2. Annotate each register: source table, row domain, type, nullability, sortedness, ordered/monotone.
91... 3. Run the passes to a fixpoint.
92... 4. Estimate cost with the `[doc: cycles.md#cost-table]` model.
93... 5. Emit.
94... 
95... **Global guard:** if the estimated cost isn't lower, an intermediate result would grow, or any pass throws an exception, emit the input unchanged.
96... 
97... | Rank | Rewrite | Gain | Risk | Safety rule (§5) | Prototype evidence |
98... |---|---|---|---|---|---|
99... | 1 | Dead-code elimination + CSE | 5–25% | very low | S1 | `h_dce` honest, 0 false alarms |
100... | 2 | GATHER composition / sinking; gather only the columns that reach OUT | 20–50% on wide plans | low | S7 | q0001, q0004 |
101... | 3 | Filter first; run element-wise ops after filters (late materialization) | 4–8× on q0001/q0004/q0007 | low | S2, S6 | q0007 2596→637 **[M]** |
102... | 4 | Sort reduction: TOPK for SORT+slice, dead SORT before order-insensitive aggregates, SORT on `sorted` keys is identity | 5–20% | med | S4, S5 | q0001, q0004, q0007 |
103... | 5 | Filter pushdown below joins (one-sided, total predicates) | 30–70% on q0004-like plans | med | S2, S3 | q0004 |
104... | 6 | Constraint rewrites: always-TRUE predicates, exactly-one-match joins | small | med | S8 | q0001 |
105... | 7 | Join algorithm choice (HJOIN↔NLJOIN by cost; stats allowed here) | small | very low | — | `h_join_swap` honest; NLJOIN is cheaper when one side has ≤ ~5 rows |
106... | 8 | Idioms: self-join+aggregate → GROUP; rank via sort; semi-join de-dup | 2–47× | **high** | S3, S4, S9 | q0003, q0005, q0006 |
107... 
108... **Skip entirely:** arithmetic re-association, join reordering, anything that uses stats for correctness.
109... **Gate:** rank 8 is enabled only after 0 defects on NULL-, tie-, scale- and empty-table-heavy data.

113... ## 4. Evaluator design (`./evaluate OPTIMIZER`)
114... 
115... 1. **Corpus.**
116...    - Programs: the 8 examples, mutants of the examples, and generated programs from a type-checked template generator over the schema (scan/filter, 1–4 joins along `refs`, GROUP aggregates, SORT/TOPK/SLICE, string/date/arithmetic) with legacy bloat added. Keep a program only if the original succeeds and gives non-empty output on at least one dataset.
117...    - Data: `gen_data.py` style, constraint-respecting, adversarial, with literals harvested from the programs, all validated by `--schema`. Plus datasets designed to make originals error.
118... 2. **Run.** One optimizer call per program, at most 4 in parallel so machine load can't cause a false "> 1 s". Then VM runs on all cores using the platform binary.
119... 3. **Compare** using the rubric in §6.
120...    - Order: a data-flow pass over the original decides whether output order is specified (`eval-proto.py: output_ordered`).
121...    - Ties: compare rows tied on the sort keys as a multiset, by running an *instrumented* original that also outputs the sort keys (still to build).
122... 4. **On a defect:** re-run once, save the repro (program, optimized program, dataset, diff) to `eval_out/`, then shrink it if time remains (stretch goal). Exit 1.
123... 5. **Budget [M]:** 8.3 ms per run means 320 checks take 1.7 s. A watchdog at 100 s stops new work and reports the verdict so far.
124... 
125... ### 4.1 Evaluation methods compared
126... 
127... | Method | How | Proves | Catches | False-alarm risk | Cost within 2 min | Use |
128... |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
129... | **Run-and-compare (differential testing)** | run original and optimized on many datasets, compare outputs | that a defect exists (a counterexample); never that there is none | anything the data exercises: NULLs, ties, order, errors, scale | low, if the comparator rules are right | ~1.7 s per 320 checks **[M]** | **primary** |
130... | **Normalize-and-compare (syntactic)** | canonicalize both programs (rename registers, DCE, sort commutative ops) and diff them | equivalence only when they normalize to identical text | nothing, if any real rewrite happened | none, but almost always "unknown" | ms | fast path: identical after normalizing ⇒ skip running the VM |
131... | **Metamorphic testing (SQLancer TLP/NoREC, EMI)** | derive related programs or data, e.g. partition on `p` / `NOT p` / `p IS NULL`, add dead code, permute rows that are unsorted by the program | defects that need no reference output | NULL three-valued-logic bugs, order assumptions, stats-as-constraint bugs | low | moderate | data-side only: NULL partitions and row permutations in the generator |
132... | **Property checks** | invariants without a reference: `ncols` same, row count same for pure projections, VM limits, optimizer time | gross failures | crashes, timeouts, limit blow-ups | none | trivial | always on |
133... | **Mutation testing of the oracle** | seed bugs into fake optimizers; measure the kill rate | the *evaluator's* recall and precision | weak data, a lenient comparator | — | ~37 s for 19 fakes **[M]** | meta-eval gate on every evaluator change |
134... | **Translation validation / math proof (Alive2, CompCert)** | encode both programs symbolically under the constraints and ask an SMT solver whether they are equivalent | **equivalence on all data** | everything, within the encoded semantics | none, if the encoding is right | days to build; may be slow per query; semantics are large (NUM rounding, Unicode UPPER, 3-valued logic) | out of scope for 2–3 h; first item in the "few days" plan |
135... | **Bounded exhaustive (small-scope hypothesis)** | enumerate all tiny databases (e.g. ≤ 3 rows, small value domains) | equivalence on every database up to that size | most semantic bugs, which show up on tiny data | none | grows exponentially with columns and values; feasible for 1–2 tables | stretch goal: NULL/''/tie value domains on 0–3 rows |
136... 
137... **Decision:** run-and-compare is the verdict. Normalize-and-compare is a fast path. Metamorphic ideas shape the data generator. Mutation testing gates the evaluator. Proofs are deferred.

141... ## 5. Safety rules: how a rewrite can produce wrong output (with doc citations)
142... 
143... | ID | Trap | Doc evidence | Probe **[M]** | Rule |
144... |---|---|---|---|---|
145... | S1 | **Adding an error.** Errors stop the program, and an optimized program that errors is a defect. Removing dead code can only remove errors, which is fine because "if the input errors, anything goes". | "Any error stops the program" `[doc: running.md#errors]`; dead `DIV x,0` still errors | F6, `b_dead_div0` caught (272) | Never add an op that may error. Deleting ops is always allowed. |
146... | S2 | **Data-dependent errors.** Type errors and DIV by 0 fire only on rows actually used, never on empty or all-NULL columns. | "Types are checked row by row ... whether a program fails can depend on its data" `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`; "DIV of NULL by 0 is NULL" (same section) | `DIV` after a `d≠0` filter OK, before it errors | An op may run only on a **subset** of the rows it originally ran on. Never push DIV/IDIV/MOD/DATEADD/overflow-prone ops or comparisons of mixed types above a filter. |
147... | S3 | **NULL keys: joins vs groups.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys (unless NULLEQ); GROUP puts NULLs together. | "A NULL key matches no key, unless ... NULLEQ" `[doc: instructions/joins.md]`; "NULL equals NULL" `[doc: instructions/grouping.md#group]` | `q0006.naive` caught (24), `b_nulleq` caught (56) | Any join↔group rewrite adds or keeps an explicit `NOT ISNULL(key)` filter. |
148... | S4 | **Order and ties.** SORT is stable, HJOIN output is ordered by (i, j), and groups are numbered by first appearance. | "Ties keep their input order" `[doc: instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys]`; "ordered by i then j" `[doc: joins.md]`; "groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance" `[doc: grouping.md#group-sets]` | `b_reverse` (172), `b_no_tiebreak` (19) | Preserve exact output order. Never swap join sides or reorder the input to GROUP/GFIRST/GMIN/GMAX. |
149... | S5 | **First-of-equals and NUM scale.** GMIN/GMAX return the first of equal values; GSUM uses the largest scale in the group; `1.0` and `1.00` print differently. | "the first of equals: of 1, 1.0 and 1.00, whichever comes first" `[doc: grouping.md#gmin-gmax]`; "1.0 and 1.00 are equal but print differently" `[doc: values.md#num-range]`; GSUM scale `[doc: grouping.md#gsum]` | F28, F5 | Keep the aggregate input order. Avoid identities that rescale (`x*1.000`, `x+0.0`): equal in value, but they change the printed text. |
150... | S6 | **Unicode changes length.** UPPER can change the character count, so UPPER and LEFT/SUBSTR don't commute. | "UPPER('straße') is 'STRASSE'" `[doc: strings.md#upper]` | `ß` in generator | Never reorder string ops relative to each other; only move them across filters and gathers. |
151... | S7 | **VM limits.** Join output counts toward limits; HJOIN/GROUP use up the work budget faster than their cycles suggest. | limits table `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | 2M-row join takes 425 ms | No rewrite may grow any intermediate result beyond the original's. |
152... | S8 | **Constraints vs stats.** Constraints hold for every dataset; stats describe one. `check` doesn't imply `not_null`. Tables without a `key` may have duplicates. | "The constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe only this one" `[doc: running.md#schema-files]`; constraint table `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | `q0004.naive` (no key on customers) | Correctness may use only key, not_null, refs, check and sorted. Stats are used only for cost. |
153... | S9 | **`sorted` covers stored order only.** It survives IDX, ascending GATHER and the left side of a join, but not the right side of HJOIN, GROUP output, or a SORT on other keys. | "the rows are stored in ascending order ... as ASC NF sorts them" `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | q0001/q0005 identity SORT | Drop a SORT only if its keys are a prefix of `sorted` ASC NF *and* the index is proven ascending from LOAD. |
154... | S10 | **Literal-only ops and OUT rules.** An element-wise op needs at least one register operand; OUT must be the last instruction and the only OUT. | `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`, `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | F23, F25 | Constant folding must not produce a literal-only op; the emitter always ends with exactly one OUT. |

188... ## 7. Unclear rules and the assumptions we make
189... 
190... How we handle each: pick the **default that can't produce a false alarm or a wrong optimization**, encode it as a check, log it, and escalate only if the choice changes more than 20% of results.
191... 
192... | # | Unclear point | Options | Default | Why | Encoded in |
193... |---|---|---|---|---|---|
194... | Q1 | When does a program "specify" order? Do tied rows count? | (a) whenever SORT/TOPK reaches OUT, strict; (b) the same, but tied rows compared as a multiset; (c) never | **(b)**; today (a) | strict order flags legal reorders of ties | `output_ordered`; tie handling still to build |
195... | Q2 | `"2.0"` vs `"2.00"`; INT `2` vs NUM `"2.0"` | text equal / numeric equal | numeric equal | "numbers within 1e-6" | `tricky_checks.py` CMP |
196... | Q3 | STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'` print like numbers | infer column types / treat as numbers | treat as numbers (documented gap) | the output JSON has no types | known gap; fix by inferring types |
197... | Q4 | Tolerance on INTs (`10000000` vs `10000001` passes) | apply to INTs / exact for INTs | apply (spec says "numbers") | follow the spec literally | CMP check |
198... | Q5 | Near zero (`0` vs `1e-7`) | relative only / add an absolute epsilon | relative only | spec says relative; correct optimizers don't change arithmetic | CMP check |
199... | Q6 | Ties at a TOPK/SLICE/GFIRST cut-off | fail / warn | warn once tie handling is built | a correct optimizer may choose another tied row | still to build |
200... | Q7 | Optimizer may use `bin/minivm`? | yes / no | no | the grader may not ship it next to `./optimize` | optimizer design |
201... | Q8 | Can stats be used? | correctness / cost only | cost only | `[doc: running.md#schema-files]` | S8 |
202... | Q9 | Optimized program hits a VM limit where the original didn't | defect / skip | defect | the program "gives a different result" (none) | O6 |
203... | Q10 | How is "faster" measured? | cycles / wall time | cycles | that's what the VM reports | P1 |

207... ## 8. Working model: how the agents talk
208... 
209... **Roles.**
210... - **Orchestrator** (main session): owns the plan and writes task cards; never writes optimizer code.
211... - **Builder** subagent: implements one rewrite per task.
212... - **Red-team** subagent: sees only the spec, docs and rubric. It writes fake optimizers and adversarial data, and never sees the optimizer code.
213... - **Checker:** the `./evaluate` script, not an LLM.
214... - **Reviewer** subagent: fresh context, for rank ≥ 5 rewrites. Its job: "name the dataset that breaks this".
215... - **Human:** approves at checkpoints and decides open questions.
216... 
217... ```
218... human ──approve/decide──▶ ORCHESTRATOR ──task.json──▶ BUILDER ──commit + build.json──▶ CHECKER(./evaluate)
219...   ▲                          │  ▲                                                        │
220...   └────escalation.json───────┘  └──────verdict.json ◀── REVIEWER ◀── report.json ◀──────┘
221...                                  RED-TEAM (spec only) ──fakes + data──▶ CHECKER (meta-eval)
222... ```
223... 
224... **Rules.**
225... - Agents communicate only through **files**, never prose summaries.
226... - Every message is a JSON document with a schema version.
227... - Prose goes only in a `notes` field.
228... - Files live under `runs/<iteration>/`.
229... 
230... ```json
231... // task.json  (orchestrator -> builder)
232... {"v":1,"task_id":"T07","goal":"sort reduction: SORT+IDX+SLICE -> IDX+TOPK",
233...  "rewrite_rank":4,"safety_rules":["S4","S5"],"files_allowed":["optimizer/passes/sort.py","tests/cases/medium/*"],
234...  "done_when":{"defects":0,"geomean_min":1.0,"opt_time_max_s":0.8},"budget":{"wall_min":15,"tokens_k":200}}
235... ```
236... ```json
237... // build.json  (builder -> checker)
238... {"v":1,"task_id":"T07","commit":"abc1234","pass":"sort_reduction","tests_added":["medium/topk_after_filter.mini"],
239...  "claims":[{"rule":"S4","why":"TOPK = first n of the same stable SORT [doc: sorting.md#topk]"}],"notes":""}
240... ```
241... ```json
242... // report.json  (checker -> everyone; also appended to notes/runs.jsonl)
243... {"v":1,"commit":"abc1234","seed":0,"checked":320,"skipped":0,"defects":0,"wall_s":1.7,
244...  "geomean_speedup":2.39,"per_program":[{"name":"q0007","speedup":4.08,"status":"OK"}],
245...  "meta":{"buggy_caught":11,"buggy_total":11,"false_alarms":0},
246...  "defect_repros":[]}
247... ```
248... ```json
249... // verdict.json  (reviewer -> orchestrator)
250... {"v":1,"commit":"abc1234","decision":"keep|revert|needs_test",
251...  "counterexample":{"program":"...","dataset":"...","expected":"...","got":"..."},"rules_checked":["S4"]}
252... ```
253... ```json
254... // escalation.json  (orchestrator -> human)
255... {"v":1,"question_id":"Q1","options":["strict","tie-multiset"],"recommended":"tie-multiset",
256...  "impact":"3/320 checks change verdict","blocking":true}
257... ```
258... 
259... **Git discipline.**
260... - One rewrite per commit.
261... - A red build gets `git revert`, never a reset or amend.
262... - Tag green checkpoints `cp1`…`cp5`.
263... - Each defect becomes a regression in `tests/regressions/`, replayed first on every run.
264... 
265... **Independence.** `evaluate/` never imports `optimizer/`; a grep check enforces this. Only the CLI and `bin/minivm` cross the boundary.

285... ## 10. Failure modes
286... 
287... | Failure | Detection | Prevention / fix |
288... |---|---|---|
289... | Rewrite breaks NULL semantics | NULL-heavy data; `b_nulleq`, `q0006.naive` | S3 |
290... | Rewrite introduces an error | O6; `b_dead_div0` | S1, S2 |
291... | Lost order or ties | order-aware comparator; `b_reverse`, `b_no_tiebreak` | S4 |
292... | Evaluator too lenient (weak data) | meta-eval misses; `BASELINE_MISSED` in `check.py` | harvest literals; more rows than every TOPK limit; ties; empty tables |
293... | Evaluator too strict (false alarm) | honest fakes (`h_*`) must pass | Q1–Q5 defaults; tie handling |
294... | Comparator type confusion | `tricky_checks.py` CMP | strict numeric format; BOOL ≠ INT (both bugs found and fixed **[M]**) |
295... | Using stats for correctness | generator deliberately violates stats | S8; lint check |
296... | VM limit blow-up | P3, O6 | S7 cost check |
297... | Optimizer > 1 s on 20k-line programs | stress test | linear passes; deadline then fall back |

113... ## 4. Evaluator design (`./evaluate OPTIMIZER`)
114... 
115... 1. **Corpus.**
116...    - Programs: the 8 examples, mutants of the examples, and generated programs from a type-checked template generator over the schema (scan/filter, 1–4 joins along `refs`, GROUP aggregates, SORT/TOPK/SLICE, string/date/arithmetic) with legacy bloat added. Keep a program only if the original succeeds and gives non-empty output on at least one dataset.
117...    - Data: `gen_data.py` style, constraint-respecting, adversarial, with literals harvested from the programs, all validated by `--schema`. Plus datasets designed to make originals error.
118... 2. **Run.** One optimizer call per program, at most 4 in parallel so machine load can't cause a false "> 1 s". Then VM runs on all cores using the platform binary.
119... 3. **Compare** using the rubric in §6.
120...    - Order: a data-flow pass over the original decides whether output order is specified (`eval-proto.py: output_ordered`).
121...    - Ties: compare rows tied on the sort keys as a multiset, by running an *instrumented* original that also outputs the sort keys (still to build).
122... 4. **On a defect:** re-run once, save the repro (program, optimized program, dataset, diff) to `eval_out/`, then shrink it if time remains (stretch goal). Exit 1.
123... 5. **Budget [M]:** 8.3 ms per run means 320 checks take 1.7 s. A watchdog at 100 s stops new work and reports the verdict so far.
124... 
125... ### 4.1 Evaluation methods compared
126... 
127... | Method | How | Proves | Catches | False-alarm risk | Cost within 2 min | Use |
128... |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
129... | **Run-and-compare (differential testing)** | run original and optimized on many datasets, compare outputs | that a defect exists (a counterexample); never that there is none | anything the data exercises: NULLs, ties, order, errors, scale | low, if the comparator rules are right | ~1.7 s per 320 checks **[M]** | **primary** |
130... | **Normalize-and-compare (syntactic)** | canonicalize both programs (rename registers, DCE, sort commutative ops) and diff them | equivalence only when they normalize to identical text | nothing, if any real rewrite happened | none, but almost always "unknown" | ms | fast path: identical after normalizing ⇒ skip running the VM |
131... | **Metamorphic testing (SQLancer TLP/NoREC, EMI)** | derive related programs or data, e.g. partition on `p` / `NOT p` / `p IS NULL`, add dead code, permute rows that are unsorted by the program | defects that need no reference output | NULL three-valued-logic bugs, order assumptions, stats-as-constraint bugs | low | moderate | data-side only: NULL partitions and row permutations in the generator |
132... | **Property checks** | invariants without a reference: `ncols` same, row count same for pure projections, VM limits, optimizer time | gross failures | crashes, timeouts, limit blow-ups | none | trivial | always on |
133... | **Mutation testing of the oracle** | seed bugs into fake optimizers; measure the kill rate | the *evaluator's* recall and precision | weak data, a lenient comparator | — | ~37 s for 19 fakes **[M]** | meta-eval gate on every evaluator change |
134... | **Translation validation / math proof (Alive2, CompCert)** | encode both programs symbolically under the constraints and ask an SMT solver whether they are equivalent | **equivalence on all data** | everything, within the encoded semantics | none, if the encoding is right | days to build; may be slow per query; semantics are large (NUM rounding, Unicode UPPER, 3-valued logic) | out of scope for 2–3 h; first item in the "few days" plan |
135... | **Bounded exhaustive (small-scope hypothesis)** | enumerate all tiny databases (e.g. ≤ 3 rows, small value domains) | equivalence on every database up to that size | most semantic bugs, which show up on tiny data | none | grows exponentially with columns and values; feasible for 1–2 tables | stretch goal: NULL/''/tie value domains on 0–3 rows |
136... 
137... **Decision:** run-and-compare is the verdict. Normalize-and-compare is a fast path. Metamorphic ideas shape the data generator. Mutation testing gates the evaluator. Proofs are deferred.

141... ## 5. Safety rules: how a rewrite can produce wrong output (with doc citations)
142... 
143... | ID | Trap | Doc evidence | Probe **[M]** | Rule |
144... |---|---|---|---|---|
145... | S1 | **Adding an error.** Errors stop the program, and an optimized program that errors is a defect. Removing dead code can only remove errors, which is fine because "if the input errors, anything goes". | "Any error stops the program" `[doc: running.md#errors]`; dead `DIV x,0` still errors | F6, `b_dead_div0` caught (272) | Never add an op that may error. Deleting ops is always allowed. |
146... | S2 | **Data-dependent errors.** Type errors and DIV by 0 fire only on rows actually used, never on empty or all-NULL columns. | "Types are checked row by row ... whether a program fails can depend on its data" `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`; "DIV of NULL by 0 is NULL" (same section) | `DIV` after a `d≠0` filter OK, before it errors | An op may run only on a **subset** of the rows it originally ran on. Never push DIV/IDIV/MOD/DATEADD/overflow-prone ops or comparisons of mixed types above a filter. |
147... | S3 | **NULL keys: joins vs groups.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys (unless NULLEQ); GROUP puts NULLs together. | "A NULL key matches no key, unless ... NULLEQ" `[doc: instructions/joins.md]`; "NULL equals NULL" `[doc: instructions/grouping.md#group]` | `q0006.naive` caught (24), `b_nulleq` caught (56) | Any join↔group rewrite adds or keeps an explicit `NOT ISNULL(key)` filter. |
148... | S4 | **Order and ties.** SORT is stable, HJOIN output is ordered by (i, j), and groups are numbered by first appearance. | "Ties keep their input order" `[doc: instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys]`; "ordered by i then j" `[doc: joins.md]`; "groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance" `[doc: grouping.md#group-sets]` | `b_reverse` (172), `b_no_tiebreak` (19) | Preserve exact output order. Never swap join sides or reorder the input to GROUP/GFIRST/GMIN/GMAX. |
149... | S5 | **First-of-equals and NUM scale.** GMIN/GMAX return the first of equal values; GSUM uses the largest scale in the group; `1.0` and `1.00` print differently. | "the first of equals: of 1, 1.0 and 1.00, whichever comes first" `[doc: grouping.md#gmin-gmax]`; "1.0 and 1.00 are equal but print differently" `[doc: values.md#num-range]`; GSUM scale `[doc: grouping.md#gsum]` | F28, F5 | Keep the aggregate input order. Avoid identities that rescale (`x*1.000`, `x+0.0`): equal in value, but they change the printed text. |
150... | S6 | **Unicode changes length.** UPPER can change the character count, so UPPER and LEFT/SUBSTR don't commute. | "UPPER('straße') is 'STRASSE'" `[doc: strings.md#upper]` | `ß` in generator | Never reorder string ops relative to each other; only move them across filters and gathers. |
151... | S7 | **VM limits.** Join output counts toward limits; HJOIN/GROUP use up the work budget faster than their cycles suggest. | limits table `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | 2M-row join takes 425 ms | No rewrite may grow any intermediate result beyond the original's. |
152... | S8 | **Constraints vs stats.** Constraints hold for every dataset; stats describe one. `check` doesn't imply `not_null`. Tables without a `key` may have duplicates. | "The constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe only this one" `[doc: running.md#schema-files]`; constraint table `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | `q0004.naive` (no key on customers) | Correctness may use only key, not_null, refs, check and sorted. Stats are used only for cost. |
153... | S9 | **`sorted` covers stored order only.** It survives IDX, ascending GATHER and the left side of a join, but not the right side of HJOIN, GROUP output, or a SORT on other keys. | "the rows are stored in ascending order ... as ASC NF sorts them" `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | q0001/q0005 identity SORT | Drop a SORT only if its keys are a prefix of `sorted` ASC NF *and* the index is proven ascending from LOAD. |
154... | S10 | **Literal-only ops and OUT rules.** An element-wise op needs at least one register operand; OUT must be the last instruction and the only OUT. | `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`, `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | F23, F25 | Constant folding must not produce a literal-only op; the emitter always ends with exactly one OUT. |

188... ## 7. Unclear rules and the assumptions we make
189... 
190... How we handle each: pick the **default that can't produce a false alarm or a wrong optimization**, encode it as a check, log it, and escalate only if the choice changes more than 20% of results.
191... 
192... | # | Unclear point | Options | Default | Why | Encoded in |
193... |---|---|---|---|---|---|
194... | Q1 | When does a program "specify" order? Do tied rows count? | (a) whenever SORT/TOPK reaches OUT, strict; (b) the same, but tied rows compared as a multiset; (c) never | **(b)**; today (a) | strict order flags legal reorders of ties | `output_ordered`; tie handling still to build |
195... | Q2 | `"2.0"` vs `"2.00"`; INT `2` vs NUM `"2.0"` | text equal / numeric equal | numeric equal | "numbers within 1e-6" | `tricky_checks.py` CMP |
196... | Q3 | STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'` print like numbers | infer column types / treat as numbers | treat as numbers (documented gap) | the output JSON has no types | known gap; fix by inferring types |
197... | Q4 | Tolerance on INTs (`10000000` vs `10000001` passes) | apply to INTs / exact for INTs | apply (spec says "numbers") | follow the spec literally | CMP check |
198... | Q5 | Near zero (`0` vs `1e-7`) | relative only / add an absolute epsilon | relative only | spec says relative; correct optimizers don't change arithmetic | CMP check |
199... | Q6 | Ties at a TOPK/SLICE/GFIRST cut-off | fail / warn | warn once tie handling is built | a correct optimizer may choose another tied row | still to build |
200... | Q7 | Optimizer may use `bin/minivm`? | yes / no | no | the grader may not ship it next to `./optimize` | optimizer design |
201... | Q8 | Can stats be used? | correctness / cost only | cost only | `[doc: running.md#schema-files]` | S8 |
202... | Q9 | Optimized program hits a VM limit where the original didn't | defect / skip | defect | the program "gives a different result" (none) | O6 |
203... | Q10 | How is "faster" measured? | cycles / wall time | cycles | that's what the VM reports | P1 |

207... ## 8. Working model: how the agents talk
208... 
209... **Roles.**
210... - **Orchestrator** (main session): owns the plan and writes task cards; never writes optimizer code.
211... - **Builder** subagent: implements one rewrite per task.
212... - **Red-team** subagent: sees only the spec, docs and rubric. It writes fake optimizers and adversarial data, and never sees the optimizer code.
213... - **Checker:** the `./evaluate` script, not an LLM.
214... - **Reviewer** subagent: fresh context, for rank ≥ 5 rewrites. Its job: "name the dataset that breaks this".
215... - **Human:** approves at checkpoints and decides open questions.
216... 
217... ```
218... human ──approve/decide──▶ ORCHESTRATOR ──task.json──▶ BUILDER ──commit + build.json──▶ CHECKER(./evaluate)
219...   ▲                          │  ▲                                                        │
220...   └────escalation.json───────┘  └──────verdict.json ◀── REVIEWER ◀── report.json ◀──────┘
221...                                  RED-TEAM (spec only) ──fakes + data──▶ CHECKER (meta-eval)
222... ```
223... 
224... **Rules.**
225... - Agents communicate only through **files**, never prose summaries.
226... - Every message is a JSON document with a schema version.
227... - Prose goes only in a `notes` field.
228... - Files live under `runs/<iteration>/`.
229... 
230... ```json
231... // task.json  (orchestrator -> builder)
232... {"v":1,"task_id":"T07","goal":"sort reduction: SORT+IDX+SLICE -> IDX+TOPK",
233...  "rewrite_rank":4,"safety_rules":["S4","S5"],"files_allowed":["optimizer/passes/sort.py","tests/cases/medium/*"],
234...  "done_when":{"defects":0,"geomean_min":1.0,"opt_time_max_s":0.8},"budget":{"wall_min":15,"tokens_k":200}}
235... ```
236... ```json
237... // build.json  (builder -> checker)
238... {"v":1,"task_id":"T07","commit":"abc1234","pass":"sort_reduction","tests_added":["medium/topk_after_filter.mini"],
239...  "claims":[{"rule":"S4","why":"TOPK = first n of the same stable SORT [doc: sorting.md#topk]"}],"notes":""}

244...  "geomean_speedup":2.39,"per_program":[{"name":"q0007","speedup":4.08,"status":"OK"}],

259... **Git discipline.**
260... - One rewrite per commit.
261... - A red build gets `git revert`, never a reset or amend.
262... - Tag green checkpoints `cp1`…`cp5`.
263... - Each defect becomes a regression in `tests/regressions/`, replayed first on every run.
264... 
265... **Independence.** `evaluate/` never imports `optimizer/`; a grep check enforces this. Only the CLI and `bin/minivm` cross the boundary.

285... ## 10. Failure modes
286... 
287... | Failure | Detection | Prevention / fix |
288... |---|---|---|
289... | Rewrite breaks NULL semantics | NULL-heavy data; `b_nulleq`, `q0006.naive` | S3 |
290... | Rewrite introduces an error | O6; `b_dead_div0` | S1, S2 |
291... | Lost order or ties | order-aware comparator; `b_reverse`, `b_no_tiebreak` | S4 |
292... | Evaluator too lenient (weak data) | meta-eval misses; `BASELINE_MISSED` in `check.py` | harvest literals; more rows than every TOPK limit; ties; empty tables |
293... | Evaluator too strict (false alarm) | honest fakes (`h_*`) must pass | Q1–Q5 defaults; tie handling |
294... | Comparator type confusion | `tricky_checks.py` CMP | strict numeric format; BOOL ≠ INT (both bugs found and fixed **[M]**) |
295... | Using stats for correctness | generator deliberately violates stats | S8; lint check |
296... | VM limit blow-up | P3, O6 | S7 cost check |
297... | Optimizer > 1 s on 20k-line programs | stress test | linear passes; deadline then fall back |
298... | Evaluator > 2 min | wall time in report | platform binary, watchdog, limits on corpus size |
299... | Overfitting to the 8 examples | held-out generated programs | general passes; no matching on names |
300... | Shared bug in optimizer and evaluator | independence grep check | separate parsers |

47... ## What we learned
48... 1. **The biggest wins are generic, not clever.** Filter before joining and before building strings. Gather only the columns that reach `OUT`. Delete dead code. Use TOPK instead of SORT followed by a slice. These gave most of q0001, q0004 and q0007 (4–8.5×). Replacing a self-join with GROUP is the only big structural rewrite (q0003, q0006), and it is also the riskiest.
49... 2. **Rewrites must rely on constraints, never on stats.**
50...    - Exactly one match is safe for `not_null` + `refs` to a key.
51...    - A SORT is a no-op on a `sorted` table.
52...    - `customers` has no key, so a join to it can multiply rows. The naive q0004, which assumes unique `c_id`, is wrong on data where `c_id` repeats.
53... 3. **NULL semantics are the main trap.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys, but GROUP puts NULLs together. NULLIFE turns `''` into NULL. IS is never NULL. Every self-join→GROUP rewrite needs an explicit NULL-key filter.
54... 4. **Safety rule for rewrites:** an operation may only run on a *subset* of the rows it originally ran on. Removing work can only remove errors, which is allowed because "if the input program errors, anything goes".
55... 5. **Weak data hides bugs.**
56...    - Two broken q0007 variants (TOPK 4 instead of 5, flipped tie-break) passed the example data. It has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts.
57...    - The q0004 naive baseline went uncaught until the generator planted the programs' own literals: no category was ever `'KITCHEN'`, so every result was empty.

63...    - JSON `true` must never equal `1`.
64...    - Remaining ambiguity: STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'`.
65... 8. **Test the tester, and test it with evidence.** An evaluator that reports 0 defects proves nothing until it has caught seeded bugs and passed honest-but-different optimizers. Honest examples include renaming registers, INT→NUM scale changes, and 1e-10 drift.
66... 9. **Calling the platform binary directly is 4.6× faster than the `bin/minivm` wrapper** (8.3 ms vs 38.6 ms per run, identical output). This leaves the 2-minute evaluator budget roomy: about 14k VM runs fit in 2 minutes even sequentially, and many more in parallel on 16 cores.

36... ## Results (measured with `bin/minivm`)
37... - **Hand-optimized speedups:** 3.14× geomean cycle reduction on `examples/data.json`. Larger datasets speed up much more, because the originals' quadratic self-joins grow with the data.
38... 
39...   | Program | q0001 | q0002 | q0003 | q0004 | q0005 | q0006 | q0007 | q0008 |
40...   |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
41...   | Speedup on example data | 8.1× | 1.8× | 3.0× | 8.5× | 1.7× | 3.0× | 4.1× | 1.2× |
42...   | Speedup on large data | 4.5× | 1.8× | 37× | 47× | 2.2× | 20× | 8.3× | 1.3× |
43... 
44... - **Correctness:** all 8 hand-optimized programs match the originals on all 40 datasets, and all 8 naive baselines are caught.
45... - **Evaluator:** catches 11 of 11 buggy fakes with 0 false alarms on 8 honest ones. A full run takes 1.7 s.
46... 
47... ## What we learned
48... 1. **The biggest wins are generic, not clever.** Filter before joining and before building strings. Gather only the columns that reach `OUT`. Delete dead code. Use TOPK instead of SORT followed by a slice. These gave most of q0001, q0004 and q0007 (4–8.5×). Replacing a self-join with GROUP is the only big structural rewrite (q0003, q0006), and it is also the riskiest.
49... 2. **Rewrites must rely on constraints, never on stats.**
50...    - Exactly one match is safe for `not_null` + `refs` to a key.
51...    - A SORT is a no-op on a `sorted` table.
52...    - `customers` has no key, so a join to it can multiply rows. The naive q0004, which assumes unique `c_id`, is wrong on data where `c_id` repeats.
53... 3. **NULL semantics are the main trap.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys, but GROUP puts NULLs together. NULLIFE turns `''` into NULL. IS is never NULL. Every self-join→GROUP rewrite needs an explicit NULL-key filter.
54... 4. **Safety rule for rewrites:** an operation may only run on a *subset* of the rows it originally ran on. Removing work can only remove errors, which is allowed because "if the input program errors, anything goes".
55... 5. **Weak data hides bugs.**
56...    - Two broken q0007 variants (TOPK 4 instead of 5, flipped tie-break) passed the example data. It has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts.
57...    - The q0004 naive baseline went uncaught until the generator planted the programs' own literals: no category was ever `'KITCHEN'`, so every result was empty.
58...    - Fix: harvest literals and their ±1 neighbours, and generate more rows than every TOPK limit, plus ties.
59... 6. **Multiset comparison alone is too lenient.** It missed a reversed-rows bug and barely caught sort-key bugs (4 and 2 defects). The order rule raised these to 172, 134 and 19 defects with no new false alarms.
60... 7. **The output JSON has no types.**
61...    - STR `"2.00"` prints like a NUM.
62...    - Only text minivm actually prints as a number (`-?\d+(\.\d+)?`) may be compared numerically; otherwise a TRIM bug on `'1.0 '` would hide.
63...    - JSON `true` must never equal `1`.
64...    - Remaining ambiguity: STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'`.
65... 8. **Test the tester, and test it with evidence.** An evaluator that reports 0 defects proves nothing until it has caught seeded bugs and passed honest-but-different optimizers. Honest examples include renaming registers, INT→NUM scale changes, and 1e-10 drift.
66... 9. **Calling the platform binary directly is 4.6× faster than the `bin/minivm` wrapper** (8.3 ms vs 38.6 ms per run, identical output). This leaves the 2-minute evaluator budget roomy: about 14k VM runs fit in 2 minutes even sequentially, and many more in parallel on 16 cores.
67... 
68... ## Known gaps (next steps for the real build)
69... - **Programs:** only the 8 example programs are tested. There is no random program generator yet, and only the example schema is used.
70... - **Error paths:** no generated dataset makes an original program error, so the "anything goes" path is untested.
71... - **Ties:** rows that tie on the sort keys are still compared in order, so an optimizer that legally reorders ties would be flagged (open question Q1).
72... - **Tolerance:** the 1e-6 relative tolerance also applies to INTs, so `10000000` vs `10000001` passes.

3... # Cycles
4... 
5... This page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum
6... of its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`
7... ([Running](running.md#command-line)).
8... 
9... ## Base cost
10... 
11... Every instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the
12... [cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.
13... 
14... A run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the
15... [work limit](running.md#program-rules).
16... 
17... ## String bytes
18... 
19... The string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and
20... 0 otherwise (including `NULL`).
21... 
22... An [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)
23... costs, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:
24... 
25... | Instructions | Base per element |
26... |---|---|
27... | `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |
28... | `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |
29... | every other element-wise instruction | 1 |
30... 
31... | Instructions | String bytes per element |
32... |---|---|
33... | comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter operand |
34... | `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |
35... | `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |
36... | every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
37... 
38... A literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.
39... 
40... ## Comparisons
41... 
42... `SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys
43... ([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows
44... costs, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the
45... shorter string.
46... 
47... For example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the
48... rows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys
49... `s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0
50... for the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one
51... comparison:
52... 
53... ```text
54... LOAD s, t.s
55... LOAD n, t.n
56... SORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL
57... OUT  o
58... ```
59... 
60... costs (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.
61... 
62... ## Cost table
63... 
64... Cycles beyond the base 4 of each instruction:
65... 
66... | Instruction | Cycles |
67... |---|---|
68... | [`ADD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`SUB`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`MUL`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`NEG`](instructions/arithmetic.md#neg) [`WRAP`](instructions/arithmetic.md#wrap) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
69... | [`DIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#div) [`IDIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#idiv) [`MOD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#mod) | 6 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
70... | [`TRUNC`](instructions/arithmetic.md#trunc) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
71... | [`EQ`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`NE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand |
72... | [`AND`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`OR`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`NOT`](instructions/logic.md#not) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
73... | [`ISNULL`](instructions/logic.md#isnull) [`NVL`](instructions/logic.md#nvl) [`IF`](instructions/logic.md#if) [`NULLIF`](instructions/logic.md#nullif) [`NULLIFE`](instructions/logic.md#nullife) | 1 per element |
74... | [`UPPER`](instructions/strings.md#upper) [`RTRIM`](instructions/strings.md#rtrim-trim) [`TRIM`](instructions/strings.md#rtrim-trim) [`LEFT`](instructions/strings.md#left) [`SUBSTR`](instructions/strings.md#substr) [`CAT`](instructions/strings.md#cat) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
75... | [`LEN`](instructions/strings.md#len) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of its operand |
76... | [`YEAR`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`MONTH`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DAY`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DOW`](instructions/dates.md#dow) [`DATEADD`](instructions/dates.md#dateadd) [`DATEDIFF`](instructions/dates.md#datediff) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
77... | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) [`FILL`](instructions/columns.md#fill) [`IOTA`](instructions/columns.md#iota) [`GATHER`](instructions/columns.md#gather) [`SLICE`](instructions/columns.md#slice) | 1 per value produced |
78... | [`IDX`](instructions/columns.md#idx) | 1 per input value |
79... | [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a stable top-down merge sort |
80... | [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#topk) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a bounded insertion buffer (each row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search), plus 1 per buffered row shifted |
81... | [`NLJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string key; plus 2 per output pair |
82... | [`HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes; plus 2 per output pair |
83... | [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) | per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys |
84... | [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md#gall) [`GID`](instructions/grouping.md#gid) [`GFIRST`](instructions/grouping.md#gfirst) | 1 per row |
85... | [`GCOUNT`](instructions/grouping.md#gcount) [`GCOUNTV`](instructions/grouping.md#gcountv) [`GSUM`](instructions/grouping.md#gsum) | 2 per row |
86... | [`GMIN`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) [`GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) | 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string |
87... | [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out) | nothing |
88... 
89... ## Example
90... 
91... On a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `'ab'`, `'cde'`, `NULL`:
92... 
93... ```text
94... LOAD  x, t.s
95... UPPER u, x
96... EQ    e, u, 'AB'
97... OUT   e
98... ```
99... 
100... | Instruction | Cost | Cycles |
101... |---|---|---|
102... | `LOAD x, t.s` | 4 + 3 values | 7 |
103... | `UPPER u, x` | 4 + (1 + 2 + 2) + (1 + 3 + 3) + (1 + 0 + 0) | 17 |
104... | `EQ e, u, 'AB'` | 4 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2) + (1 + 0) | 11 |
105... | `OUT e` | 4 | 4 |
106... | total | | 39 |
107... 
108... `UPPER` pays for the bytes of its operand and of its result; `EQ` pays for the
109... shorter of `u` and the literal `'AB'` at each row. `bin/minivm` prints
110... `{"ncols":1,"rows":[[true],[false],[null]],"cycles":39}`.

3... # Running
4... 
5... This page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,
6... how to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it
7... reads.
8... 
9... ## Program rules
10... 
11... The last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out).
12... 
13... | Limit | Value |
14... |---|---|
15... | instructions per program | at most 20,000 |
16... | values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |
17... | values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string counts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |
18... | work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |
19... | rows per table | at most 10,000 |
20... | program file | at most 4 MiB |
21... | table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |
22... 
23... The work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`
24... and `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles
25... suggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other
26... limit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that
27... finishes.
28... 
29... ## Errors
30... 
31... Any error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr
32... and `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.
33... 
34... ## Command line
35... 
36... ```sh
37... bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json
38... bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json
39... ```
40... 
41... runs the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in
42... `TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:
43... 
44... ```json
45... {"ncols": N, "rows": [...], "cycles": C}
46... ```
47... 
48... - `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.
49... - `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.
50...   `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,
51...   or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keeps
52...   its digits after the point (`"250.00"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string
53...   `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
54... - `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).
55... 
56... | Exit status | Meaning |
57... |---|---|
58... | 0 | success; the result is on stdout |
59... | 1 | error; the message is on stderr |
60... | 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |
61... 
62... With the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as
63... `over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:
64... 
65... ```sh
66... $ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json
67... {"ncols":2,"rows":[[1,"250.00"]],"cycles":42}
68... ```
69... 
70... `bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-files)
71... as one line of JSON instead of running a program.
72... 
73... A program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:
74... 
75... ```text
76... LOAD d, orders.o_date
77... GT   m, d, 5
78... OUT  m
79... ```
80... 
81... ```sh
82... $ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json
83... error: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE
84... ```
85... 
86... ## Table sets
87... 
88... A table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:
89... 
90... ```json
91... {"<table>": {"columns": [{"name": "c", "type": "INT|NUM|STR|DATE"}], "rows": [[...], ...]}}
92... ```
93... 
94... - Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting
95...   with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.
96... - `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `DATE`.
97... - `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.
98...   A table without `rows` is empty.
99... - A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).
100... - Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated key.
101... - A table holds at most 10,000 rows.
102... - INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.
103... - NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the
104...   [NUM range](values.md#num-range).
105... - Dates are strings `"YYYY-MM-DD"`, years 0001 to 9999.
106... - JSON `null` is `NULL`.
107... 
108... A program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load)).
109... 
110... ### Constraints
111... 
112... A table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared
113... constraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an error.
114... 
115... | Key | Example | Guarantee |
116... |---|---|---|
117... | `key` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows agree on all of them |
118... | `not_null` | `["p_price"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |
119... | `refs` | `{"l_prod": "products.p_id"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |
120... | `check` | `{"l_qty": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |
121... | `sorted` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of the columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |
122... 
123... Values are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and
124... `1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard
125... to case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. A table may refer to itself.
126... 
127... ```json
128... {
129...   "orders": {"columns": [{"name": "o_id", "type": "INT"}], "key": ["o_id"], "rows": [[1], [2]]},
130...   "lines": {
131...     "columns": [{"name": "l_order", "type": "INT"}, {"name": "l_qty", "type": "INT"}],
132...     "refs": {"l_order": "orders.o_id"}, "check": {"l_qty": [1, null]}, "sorted": ["l_order"],
133...     "rows": [[1, 3], [1, 1], [2, 5]]
134...   }
135... }
136... ```
137... 
138... ### Example
139... 
140... ```json
141... {
142...   "orders": {
143...     "columns": [
144...       {"name": "o_id",     "type": "INT"},
145...       {"name": "o_amt",    "type": "NUM"},
146...       {"name": "o_date",   "type": "DATE"},
147...       {"name": "o_status", "type": "STR"}
148...     ],
149...     "rows": [
150...       [1, 250.00,   "2024-01-31", "shipped"],
151...       [2, "99.5",   "2024-02-01", ""],
152...       [3, null,     "2024-02-03", null]
153...     ]
154...   }
155... }
156... ```
157... 
158... ## Schema files
159... 
160... `bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` describes a table set without its rows: each table's
161... columns and [constraints](#constraints), as in the table set, plus a `stats` object
162... summarizing its rows:
163... 
164... ```json
165... {"<table>": {"columns": [...], "key": [...], ..., "stats": {"rows": N, "columns": {"<column>": {"nulls": N, "distinct": N, "min": v, "max": v, "common": [[v, N], ...], ...}}}}}
166... ```
167... 
168... The constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe only this one.
169... 
170... | Stats field | Meaning |
171... |---|---|
172... | `rows` | rows in the table |
173... | `nulls` | `NULL` values in the column |
174... | `distinct` | distinct non-NULL values, compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering) |
175... | `min`, `max` | least and greatest non-NULL value; `null` if there is none |
176... | `avg_bytes` | STR only: mean bytes of the non-NULL values, rounded to 2 decimal places; 0 if there are none |
177... | `common` | up to 8 values that occur more than once, most frequent first (ties in value order), with their counts |
178... | `histogram` | INT, NUM and DATE only, if any value is non-NULL: 11 bounds of 10 equal-count buckets of the sorted non-NULL values, from `min` to `max` |
179... "

3... # Cycles
4... 
5... This page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum
6... of its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`
7... ([Running](running.md#command-line)).
8... 
9... ## Base cost
10... 
11... Every instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the
12... [cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.
13... 
14... A run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the
15... [work limit](running.md#program-rules).
16... 
17... ## String bytes
18... 
19... The string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and
20... 0 otherwise (including `NULL`).
21... 
22... An [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)
23... costs, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:
24... 
25... | Instructions | Base per element |
26... |---|---|
27... | `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |
28... | `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |
29... | every other element-wise instruction | 1 |
30... 
31... | Instructions | String bytes per element |
32... |---|---|
33... | comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter operand |
34... | `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |
35... | `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |
36... | every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
37... 
38... A literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.
39... 
40... ## Comparisons
41... 
42... `SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys
43... ([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows
44... costs, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the
45... shorter string.
46... 
47... For example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the
48... rows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys
49... `s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0
50... for the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one
51... comparison:
52... 
53... ```text
54... LOAD s, t.s
55... LOAD n, t.n
56... SORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL
57... OUT  o
58... ```
59... 
60... costs (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.
61... 
62... ## Cost table
63... 
64... Cycles beyond the base 4 of each instruction:
65... 
66... | Instruction | Cycles |
67... |---|---|
68... | [`ADD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`SUB`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`MUL`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`NEG`](instructions/arithmetic.md#neg) [`WRAP`](instructions/arithmetic.md#wrap) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
69... | [`DIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#div) [`IDIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#idiv) [`MOD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#mod) | 6 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
70... | [`TRUNC`](instructions/arithmetic.md#trunc) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
71... | [`EQ`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`NE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand |
72... | [`AND`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`OR`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`NOT`](instructions/logic.md#not) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
73... | [`ISNULL`](instructions/logic.md#isnull) [`NVL`](instructions/logic.md#nvl) [`IF`](instructions/logic.md#if) [`NULLIF`](instructions/logic.md#nullif) [`NULLIFE`](instructions/logic.md#nullife) | 1 per element |
74... | [`UPPER`](instructions/strings.md#upper) [`RTRIM`](instructions/strings.md#rtrim-trim) [`TRIM`](instructions/strings.md#rtrim-trim) [`LEFT`](instructions/strings.md#left) [`SUBSTR`](instructions/strings.md#substr) [`CAT`](instructions/strings.md#cat) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
75... | [`LEN`](instructions/strings.md#len) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of its operand |
76... | [`YEAR`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`MONTH`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DAY`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DOW`](instructions/dates.md#dow) [`DATEADD`](instructions/dates.md#dateadd) [`DATEDIFF`](instructions/dates.md#datediff) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
77... | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) [`FILL`](instructions/columns.md#fill) [`IOTA`](instructions/columns.md#iota) [`GATHER`](instructions/columns.md#gather) [`SLICE`](instructions/columns.md#slice) | 1 per value produced |
78... | [`IDX`](instructions/columns.md#idx) | 1 per input value |
79... | [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a stable top-down merge sort |
80... | [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#topk) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a bounded insertion buffer (each row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search), plus 1 per buffered row shifted |
81... | [`NLJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string key; plus 2 per output pair |
82... | [`HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes; plus 2 per output pair |
83... | [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) | per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys |
84... | [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md#gall) [`GID`](instructions/grouping.md#gid) [`GFIRST`](instructions/grouping.md#gfirst) | 1 per row |
85... | [`GCOUNT`](instructions/grouping.md#gcount) [`GCOUNTV`](instructions/grouping.md#gcountv) [`GSUM`](instructions/grouping.md#gsum) | 2 per row |
86... | [`GMIN`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) [`GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) | 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string |
87... | [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out) | nothing |
88... 
89... ## Example
90... 
91... On a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `'ab'`, `'cde'`, `NULL`:
92... 
93... ```text
94... LOAD  x, t.s
95... UPPER u, x
96... EQ    e, u, 'AB'
97... OUT   e
98... ```
99... 
100... | Instruction | Cost | Cycles |
101... |---|---|---|
102... | `LOAD x, t.s` | 4 + 3 values | 7 |
103... | `UPPER u, x` | 4 + (1 + 2 + 2) + (1 + 3 + 3) + (1 + 0 + 0) | 17 |
104... | `EQ e, u, 'AB'` | 4 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2) + (1 + 0) | 11 |
105... | `OUT e` | 4 | 4 |
106... | total | | 39 |
107... 
108... `UPPER` pays for the bytes of its operand and of its result; `EQ` pays for the
109... shorter of `u` and the literal `'AB'` at each row. `bin/minivm` prints
110... `{"ncols":1,"rows":[[true],[false],[null]],"cycles":39}`.
111... "
